title: Personal data; childhood and move to Avery
description: Interviewer Cathy Naugle fills out a personal data record with Ruth Lindow, covering her name, birth in Denver in 1910, nicknames, and arrival in Avery, Idaho, by train in August 1917. Ruth explains returning to Denver and attending school in Missoula because Avery's high school was unaccredited.

title: Mother and stepfather's courtship; blended family
description: Ruth tells how her mother Alma and stepfather, childhood sweethearts separated when his family moved to Pasadena, reunited after both were widowed and married in Denver in 1917 before moving to Kelly Creek near Avery. She describes the cabins built to house the blended family and her mother's work as a seamstress.

title: Parents' and brother's lives; work history
description: Ruth gives details about her Swedish father John Larson, an upholsterer and streetcar motorman in Denver, her German-born mother, and her brother Stanford's Forest Service career. She then recounts her own brief marriage in 1927, her daughter Betty Jean, and her many jobs: lifeguard, waitress, Forest Service camp cook, school district clerk for 26 years, and postmaster for 32 years.

title: Retirement; house renovation; community roles
description: Ruth explains retiring in 1969 to fish and paint and care for her mother, buying the sunny East Avery house, and renovating it with her grandson. She lists her current civic roles: writing the Avery news, church trustee, water and sewer district president, and citizens committee secretary, noting railroad men called her Mrs. Avery.

title: Railroad town history; water and sewer fight
description: Ruth describes Avery as a Milwaukee Railroad company town, the electrification system powered from Thompson Falls and its removal, and the Terrio family's sale of the townsite during the war. She recounts the long campaign to form a water and sewer district after the railroad's departure left the town without services.

title: Clubs, honors; school and church life; painting
description: Ruth covers her club memberships, her listing in Community Leaders of America, and the thick skin needed for volunteer work. She recalls the town's school history, her stepfather on the school board, the community church and scouts, her painting class, and repairing fishing poles during the war.

title: Family ties; flood rescue; rewards of rural life
description: Ruth reflects on her varied occupations, her daughter in Billings and the grandson who shares her love of Avery, and her helicopter rescue during the 1974 flood after a medication reaction. She closes by praising the beauty, air, fishing, and neighborly cooperation of isolated small-town life.

title: Community Involvement; Rural Life
description: Ruth Evelyn Lidlow discusses the active role of educated newcomers in supporting community institutions in Avery. She compares the opportunities for women in rural areas versus cities, advocating for the satisfaction found in communal efforts.

title: Family Life; Marriage
description: Lidlow reflects on her childhood, noting the contrast with today's expectations for constant entertainment. She shares stories about her daughter, including her early marriage and Lidlow's own decisions regarding marriage.

title: Health; Social Changes
description: Lidlow recounts her personal experiences with health and the evolution of societal attitudes towards topics like sex education. She discusses her views on marriage, influenced by her daughter's and grandchildren's experiences.

title: Economic Resilience; Women's Movement
description: The conversation turns to economic challenges, with Lidlow praising the self-sufficiency of rural communities. She also offers her perspective on the women's movement, recognizing its benefits while cautioning against extremes.

title: Personal Reflections; Faith
description: Lidlow concludes with reflections on her life satisfaction and the importance of faith. She expresses gratitude for her life in Avery and shares her hopeful outlook on the afterlife.
